title: Why Did Carlos Alcaraz Smile After Losing at 3:34 in the Morning?
summary:
Imagine playing a tennis match that ends at 3:34 in the morning. You've been running and hitting for almost four and a half hours. You lose. Would you smile?

Carlos Alcaraz did. He's one of the best tennis players in the world, with seven Grand Slam titles. But at the US Open, he lost a long, tough match to Ben Shelton. It was the latest finish in the tournament's history.

As Alcaraz walked through the tunnel, cameras caught him grinning from ear to ear. Why? Because he had been injured for more than five months. A wrist injury hurt every day. He missed the French Open and Wimbledon. He didn't even know if he could play in New York until a week before.

"I suffered, but I enjoyed," he said. "That's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling."

Alcaraz also thinks matches shouldn't end so late. "I think it's too much," he said. He wants a rule that says no match can finish after 11 p.m.

Next, he's playing for Team Europe in the Laver Cup in London. "When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," he said.
why_it_matters: It shows that losing is not the same as failing, and that taking care of your body and getting enough sleep matters for athletes — and for kids with school the next morning.

background_read: Carlos Alcaraz (a tennis star from Spain) is one of the top players in the world and has won several Grand Slam tournaments.
The US Open (a Grand Slam tournament played in New York) is famous for long matches that sometimes run late into the night, which some players say is unfair.
The Laver Cup (a team competition named after the Australian tennis legend Rod Laver) puts the best players from Europe on one team against a team from the rest of the world.
Article_Structure: WHO: Carlos Alcaraz, a top tennis player with seven Grand Slam titles, and Ben Shelton, the player who beat him.
WHAT: He lost a match that lasted almost four and a half hours and ended at 3:34 in the morning — the latest finish in the tournament's history — but he smiled anyway.
WHERE: At the US Open in New York; his next event is the Laver Cup in London.
WHY: A wrist injury had kept him out for more than five months, so just being able to play again made him happy — and he now wants a rule that no match may finish after 11 p.m.

perspectives.description: They loved his big smile after a tough loss, saying it shows good sportsmanship and how much he missed playing.
